mcqs.question: Which of the following statements correctly expresses the addition theorem for any two events A and B?

options.B: P(A \cup B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A \cap B)
options.C: P(A \cup B) = P(A) - P(B) + P(A \cap B)

mcqs.answer: P(A \cup B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A \cap B)
mcqs.explanation: The addition theorem (also called the inclusion‑exclusion principle) states that for any two events A and B, the probability of their union is the sum of their individual probabilities minus the probability of their overlap: P(A∪B)=P(A)+P(B)−P(A∩B). Option B reflects this exactly; the other options either omit the overlap term or use incorrect operations.

mcqs.learning_point: Calculate probability of A union B
mcqs.question: A standard deck of 52 cards is shuffled. Let A be the event "the drawn card is a heart" and B be the event "the drawn card is a king". What is P(A \cup B)?
mcqs.explanation: P(A)=13/52=1/4, P(B)=4/52=1/13, and the overlap (king of hearts) has probability 1/52. Using the addition theorem: P(A∪B)=1/4+1/13-1/52 = (13+4-1)/52 =16/52 =4/13. Hence option B is correct; the other fractions arise from arithmetic errors or ignoring the overlap term.

mcqs.question: Which description best defines mutually exclusive events?

options.A: Events that can occur together but have equal probabilities
options.B: Events whose occurrence together is impossible, i.e., P(A \cap B)=0
options.C: Events that are independent, so P(A \cap B)=P(A)P(B)
options.D: Events that always have the same outcome

mcqs.answer: Events whose occurrence together is impossible, i.e., P(A \cap B)=0
mcqs.explanation: Mutually exclusive (or disjoint) events cannot happen at the same time, so their intersection is empty and its probability is zero. Option B states this precisely. Option C describes independence, not mutual exclusivity, while A and D are unrelated.

mcqs.learning_point: Apply the theorem to numerical problems
mcqs.question: A fair die is rolled once. Let A be the event "an even number appears" and B be the event "the number is greater than 3". What is P(A \cup B)?
mcqs.explanation: P(A)=3/6=1/2 (even numbers 2,4,6). P(B)=3/6=1/2 (numbers 4,5,6). Intersection A∩B = {4,6} → 2/6=1/3. Using addition theorem: P(A∪B)=1/2+1/2-1/3=1-1/3=2/3. Option B matches; other options result from omitting the overlap or miscounting outcomes.

mcqs.question: Select the statement that correctly defines the addition theorem for probabilities and distinguishes it from simple addition of probabilities.

options.A: P(A \cup B)=P(A)+P(B) because the events are always independent
options.B: P(A \cup B)=P(A)+P(B)-P(A \cap B); the subtraction removes the double‑counted overlap
options.C: P(A \cup B)=P(A)\times P(B); this accounts for overlap
options.D: P(A \cup B)=\max\{P(A),P(B)\}; this ensures the larger probability dominates

mcqs.answer: P(A \cup B)=P(A)+P(B)-P(A \cap B); the subtraction removes the double‑counted overlap
mcqs.explanation: The addition theorem (inclusion‑exclusion) states that the probability of the union equals the sum of individual probabilities minus the probability of their intersection, preventing double‑counting. Option B captures this; the other options misrepresent independence, multiplication, or a max function.

mcqs.learning_point: Calculate probability of A union B
mcqs.question: A bag contains 5 red, 3 blue, and 2 green balls. Event A: drawing a red ball. Event B: drawing a green ball. What is the probability of drawing a ball that is either red or green?
mcqs.explanation: Total balls =10. P(A)=5/10=1/2, P(B)=2/10=1/5, and A and B are mutually exclusive (no ball is both red and green), so P(A∪B)=1/2+1/5=5/10+2/10=7/10. Option A is correct; the others arise from incorrect addition or ignoring exclusivity.

mcqs.question: Which pair of events below are mutually exclusive?

options.A: Rolling a 2 on a die and rolling an even number on the same die
options.B: Drawing a queen from a deck of cards and drawing a red card
options.C: Selecting a student who studies Mathematics and selecting a student who studies Physics, given that 10 students study both subjects
options.D: Getting a head on a single coin toss and getting a tail on the same toss

mcqs.answer: Getting a head on a single coin toss and getting a tail on the same toss
mcqs.explanation: A single coin toss cannot result in both head and tail simultaneously, so these events are mutually exclusive (intersection probability zero). Option A is not mutually exclusive because 2 is even; Option B overlaps (queen of hearts or diamonds); Option C overlaps because some students study both subjects.

mcqs.learning_point: Apply the theorem to numerical problems
mcqs.question: In a class of 40 students, 22 study Mathematics, 18 study Physics, and 10 study both subjects. If a student is chosen at random, what is the probability that the student studies Mathematics or Physics (or both)?
mcqs.explanation: Number studying at least one of the subjects = 22 + 18 – 10 = 30 (inclusion‑exclusion). Probability = 30/40 = 3/4. Option A matches; the other fractions result from omitting the overlap subtraction or miscalculating the total.
